ety.text: From Middle English huge, from Old French ahuge (“high, lofty, great, large, huge”), of unknown origin. One theory derives it from an underlying Old French a hoge (“at height”), from a (“at, to”) + hoge (“a hill, height”), the latter from Frankish *haug or cognate Old Norse haugr (“hill”); both from Proto-Germanic *haugaz (“hill, mound”), from Proto-Indo-European *kowkós (“hill, mound”), from the root Proto-Indo-European *kewk-, whence also English high.

ex: Both of my parents are huge supporters of animal rights.
After the children went to bed, the couple got into a huge argument.
The band's next album is going to be huge.
In our league our coach is huge!

From earlier hugge (“to embrace, clasp with the arms”) (1560), probably representing a conflation of huck (“to crouch, huddle down”) and Old Norse hugga (“to comfort, console”), from hugr (“mind, heart, thought”), from Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“mind, thought, sense”), cognate with Icelandic hugga (“to comfort”), Old English hyġe (“thought”) (whence high (Etymology 2)).

senses.d: A close embrace, especially when charged with an emotion such as affection, joy, relief, lust, anger, aggression, compassion, or the like, as opposed to being characterized by formality, equivocation or ambivalence (a half-embrace).
To crouch; to huddle as with cold.
ex: They had a slight breast work, and they hugged down behind it and waited.
bright rocks whose stain of emerald or quartz shaft of shine the starfish hugged beneath the tide .

senses.d: To embrace by holding closely, especially in the arms.
ex: Billy hugged Danny until he felt better.
They hugged for what seemed like an eternity.
to hug the shore, to hug the coastline
Gourock also boasted a pier railway, although its pier hugged the shore rather than jutting into the bay.

senses.d: To hold fast; to cling to; to cherish.
ex: We hug intellectual deformities, if they bear our names
